lesson.title: Bits and bytes
lesson.subtitle: How a device stores numbers, letters and sensor readings

video.title: Bits and bytes
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Why an Arabic SMS costs more

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up a phone showing a long Arabic message split into 3 parts; beside it, the English one in 1 part.
scenes.narration: My pupils sent a text message in Arabic, and it went as three messages. The same text in English went as one. Same phone, same length, three times the price. The reason is bits.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: bits and bytes, how every device stores numbers, words and sensor readings.

scenes.visual: A row of tiny switches, one flips on. Then two, three, eight switches with a counter of possible values.
scenes.animation: Switches flip; the counter doubles each time a switch is added.
scenes.narration: Inside a device, everything is stored as tiny switches that are on or off. Each one is a bit: a one or a zero. One bit can only say yes or no. But every extra bit doubles how many values you can make.

scenes.visual: Place values 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above five boxes; the boxes for 4 and 1 light up and add to 5.
scenes.animation: Place values pop in right to left; lit boxes add up.
scenes.narration: In binary, each place is worth double the one to its right: one, two, four, eight, sixteen, and so on. To read a binary number, add up the places that are on. One, zero, one means four, no two, and one: five.

scenes.visual: Eight boxes join into one 'byte' block. The letter A drops into one block; an Arabic letter takes two. An SMS bubble fills up.
scenes.animation: Blocks fill; the SMS bubble's counter stops at 70.
scenes.narration: Eight bits make a byte, which holds any number from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. A Latin letter, like A, is stored in one byte. An Arabic letter needs two bytes. A text message has room for a hundred and forty bytes, so an Arabic one holds only seventy letters.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds three cards: 1, 1, 0. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! In binary, what number is one, one, zero?

scenes.visual: The three cards turn over: 4 lit, 2 lit, 1 dark; a big 6 appears.
scenes.narration: Six. The places are four, two and one. Four plus two is six, and the ones place is zero.

scenes.visual: Two boards side by side; a sensor's wavy voltage becomes a staircase of numbers, finer on the ESP32.
scenes.animation: The staircase on the right has smaller steps.
scenes.narration: Bits matter for sensors too. A microcontroller turns a sensor's voltage into a number. An Arduino Uno uses ten bits, so its readings go from zero to one thousand and twenty-three. An ESP32 uses twelve bits: from zero to four thousand and ninety-five, so it sees finer steps.

scenes.visual: A thermometer beside a staircase: each step labelled 0.5 °C.
scenes.animation: The reading climbs one step at a time.
scenes.narration: What does a step mean? On a five-volt Arduino, each step is about five millivolts. With a common temperature sensor, that's about half a degree per step. More bits give finer steps, but more data to store and send.

scenes.visual: Three objects on a scale: a tiny reading, a text bubble, and a huge photo that tips the scale.
scenes.animation: Each item drops onto the scale in turn.
scenes.narration: So how big is data? A temperature reading fits in two bytes. A text message is about a hundred and forty. A phone photo is about three million. That's why a sensor can send readings all year over a slow, cheap network.

scenes.visual: Amina beside a small weather station on a pole with a SIM symbol. Thumbs-up and thumbs-down cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our weather station sends one temperature reading every ten minutes, over mobile data. Will that use a lot of data?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a switch, doubling arrows, a byte block, a fine staircase.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: No: about a hundred and fifty readings a day, a few bytes each, is tiny, even with the extra bytes every message carries. Remember: a bit is one or zero, each place doubles, eight bits make a byte, and more bits give finer readings.

scenes.visual: Groups race with dot cards; one holds up 10110 for 22. A pupil writes her age, 01101, on the board.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: binary dot cards. Give each group five cards, and race to make the numbers you call out. Finish with every pupil writing their age in binary. Next time: the microcontroller that puts all of this to work.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the places are 4, 2 and 1, so 110 is 4 + 2 = 6.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — in binary the places are 4, 2 and 1, not hundreds, tens and ones. 110 is 4 + 2 = 6.

checkpoints.prompt: A weather station sends one temperature reading every 10 minutes over mobile data. Is that a lot of data?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 144 readings a day at a few bytes each is tiny, even with each message's extra bytes.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a reading is only a few bytes. 144 a day is far less than one photo.
